name: Carry trade as taught to retail (hold a positive-swap pair)

origin.authors: Retail practice (the 'Mrs Watanabe' yen carry); crash risk documented by Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen
origin.source_title: Carry trades and currency crashes (NBER Macroeconomics Annual 2008; NBER WP 14473)

how_it_works.simple: Borrow in a currency with low interest, like the yen, and hold one with high interest, like the Australian dollar. Your broker pays you the difference every night.
how_it_works.analogy: Like borrowing money from a friend who charges almost nothing and putting it in a bank that pays a lot, as long as the exchange rate does not move against you.
how_it_works.precise: The retail version is usually one pair (AUD/JPY, NZD/JPY, USD/TRY) held long for the positive overnight swap, often with high margin. It is a concentrated form of the G10 carry factor. Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen (2008) show carry returns are negatively skewed because positions unwind suddenly when risk appetite and funding dry up.

rule: Each month, go long the pair with the largest positive interest differential among a small menu (for example AUD/JPY, NZD/JPY, USD/JPY), hold while the broker's swap is positive, and switch if another pair's differential becomes larger. No hedging.
data_needed: The retail broker's swap rates, which include a markup over the interest differential
economic_rationale: Uncovered interest parity fails on average, so high-yield currencies have tended not to depreciate enough to offset the rate gap; Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen (2008) explain the premium partly as compensation for crash risk.
why_it_might_fail: A single pair has no diversification and the crash risk does not diversify away even across portfolios (BNP 2008). They cite the dollar's sharp fall against the yen on 7 and 8 October 1998 without fundamental news. Retail swaps add a broker markup, and 30:1 margin turns a carry crash into a margin call.

reported_results.source: Brunnermeier, Nagel and Pedersen (2008), Table 2, 1 long and 1 short
reported_results.market: Highest vs lowest interest rate currency, equal weighted
reported_results.notes: Weekly average return 0.002, weekly standard deviation 0.017, skewness -0.717. Quarterly version (1986-2006) Sharpe 0.654, skewness -0.700. For comparison the US stock market Sharpe was 0.44 weekly. No transaction costs or retail swap markups. The single-pair portfolio is the closest analogue to retail carry.

post_publication_evidence: Carry suffered a large drawdown in 2008, right as the paper was published; see the fx-carry-g10 and fx-carry-volatility-timing entries for the diversified version and its later record.

relevance.reason: Testable with free daily data, but largely a concentrated duplicate of fx-carry-g10; useful to show how much single-pair risk retail traders take.
